Dockerised SQL Injection Pentest Lab

A practical documentation of building and testing a vulnerable-vs-secure web application lab in Kali Linux, following the public demo lab by Cyb3rflex. Two Node.js/Express apps run side by side on Docker Compose: one builds its SQL query by concatenating raw input (vulnerable), the other uses parameterized queries (secure).

Docker ComposeNode.js / ExpresscurlKali Linux
PHASE 1

Setting Up the Lab

After cloning the repository, I moved into the project folder and tried to install Docker Compose as a plugin.

sudo apt install docker -compose -y

My first attempt had a space between docker and -compose, which apt read as two separate things and failed. Typing the correct package name, docker-compose, installed it correctly.

Reviewing the Compose file and the vulnerable app's Dockerfile

cat docker-compose.yml

The Compose file defines two services on a shared network called labnet: vuln, built from ./vulnerable-app and published on port 3000, and safe, built from ./secure-app and published on port 4000.

cat vulnerable-app/Dockerfile find . -maxdepth 2 -type f | sort

The Dockerfile copies the application code in, exposes port 3000, and starts the app with CMD ["node","server.js"].

PHASE 2

Verifying and Building the Lab

sudo docker-compose config

Compose printed a warning that the version: "3.8" line is obsolete, but this did not stop anything from working. The resolved configuration confirmed both services, their build contexts, and port mappings.

sudo docker-compose build

Both images finished building: base layers pulled and extracted, npm install --production ran for each app, and Compose reported both images as Built.

A second build attempt failed on DNS, then docker-compose up worked

A rebuild failed with failed to fetch anonymous token... dial tcp: lookup auth.docker.io — a DNS resolution failure, not a problem with the lab files. Cancelling and running docker-compose up worked instead, since the images were already built and cached locally.

PHASE 3

Testing the Running Applications

curl -i http://localhost:4000 curl -i http://localhost:3000

Both containers answered independently once fully started: port 3000 with the vulnerable login form, port 4000 with the secure one.

Confirming the secure app uses parameterized queries

Watching the live container logs, the secure app logged each login attempt as a [PARAMETERIZED QUERY], printing the template SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ? — the user's input never becomes part of the SQL text, so it cannot change the query's structure.

PHASE 4

Attempting the SQL Injection — Unresolved / Work in Progress

This section documents an attempt that did not yet succeed. Left in rather than hidden, because the goal of this write-up is to record what actually happened, not just the parts that worked.

The lab's README suggests testing the classic authentication-bypass payload ' OR '1'='1 against the vulnerable endpoint, intended to make the WHERE clause always evaluate true.

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/vuln/login \ --data-urlencode "username=' OR '1'='1" \ --data-urlencode "password="

Sending that payload returned 401 Unauthorized — "Invalid username or password" — the opposite of what the exercise expects for a vulnerable endpoint. Not yet resolved. Next steps: check whether --data-urlencode is escaping the quotes before they reach the server, whether the app actually concatenates raw SQL, and whether the payload needs to target a different field.

PHASE 5

Final Project Structure & Troubleshooting

Command / mistakeResultCause and fix
sudo apt install docker -compose -yUnable to read composeSpace typed where a hyphen belongs
sudo docker-compose build (2nd time)DNS lookup failureCancelled, ran docker-compose up with cached images
curl right after docker-compose upCould not connectContainers still starting; retried seconds later
' OR '1'='1 payload401 UnauthorizedInjection unresolved — see Phase 4

Conclusion

This practical taught how a vulnerable and a secure version of the same login feature can run side by side with Docker Compose, and how to read a Compose file and Dockerfile before running them. Comparing the two apps' logs made the core lesson concrete: the secure app visibly logs a parameterized query with placeholders, which is what stops injected SQL from changing the query's logic. The SQL injection payload itself did not yet succeed against the vulnerable endpoint — documented honestly as unfinished work rather than a claimed result.
